title: Error Handling, Retries, and Reliable Workflows
summary: Beginners build automations that work on the happy path; professionals build automations that keep working when things go wrong, and this reliability mindset is what separates a hobby project from production. Automations fail for many reasons: an API
content:
# Error Handling, Retries, and Reliable Workflows ##### The automation that worked for six weeks An e-commerce team built an order-sync automation: Shopify order in, warehouse system out. It ran flawlessly for six weeks. Then their warehouse provider had a 40-minute outage on a Saturday afternoon. During those 40 minutes, 63 orders came in. Each one hit the warehouse API, got a `503 Service Unavailable`, and the workflow stopped. No retry. No queue. No alert — because the alert step came *after* the failing step and never ran. The team found out on Monday, from customers. Reconstructing which orders had synced took most of a day, and two got shipped twice because someone re-ran the workflow by hand without checking. Nothing about the happy path was wrong. Every failure here was a **missing failure path**. This is the day you stop building automations that work and start building automations that *keep* working — which is, precisely, the line between a hobby project and production software. ##### Why automations fail Failures are not exotic. They come from a short, predictable list: **Transient failures** — temporary, and likely to succeed if you simply try again: - `429 Too Many Requests` — you hit a rate limit. - `500` / `502` / `503` / `504` — the other service is having a bad moment. - Network timeouts and DNS blips. **Permanent failures** — retrying will fail identically forever: - `400 Bad Request` / `422 Unprocessable Entity` — your payload is wrong. - `401` / `403` — expired credential or missing scope. - `404` — the record you referenced does not exist. **Data failures** — the request is fine, the data is not: - A required field is missing or empty. - A value is the wrong type (`"forty-five"` where a number is expected). - A date fails to parse, an email is malformed. - An array you expected has zero elements. **Logic and environment failures**: - Someone renamed a spreadsheet column or deleted a Slack channel. - A duplicate arrives and violates a uniqueness constraint. - Plan quota exhausted mid-run. The reason this taxonomy matters is that **each class needs a different response.** Retrying a `400` is pointless. Alerting on every `429` is noise. Skipping a malformed record is right; skipping a failed payment is not. ##### Error handlers: try/catch for workflows Every platform gives you a structured way to catch failures instead of halting. **Make.com** attaches an **error handler route** to any module (right-click → *Add error handler*), then applies a directive: - **Resume** — substitute a fallback value and carry on as if the module succeeded. Ideal for optional enrichment. - **Ignore** — skip this bundle, continue with the next. Ideal for per-record data problems. - **Rollback** — stop the scenario and undo where possible. For transactional integrity. - **Commit** — stop but keep what succeeded. - **Break** — park the failed bundle in the *incomplete executions* queue for automatic or manual retry later. This is the closest thing to a dead-letter queue and it is enormously useful. **n8n** offers per-node **Retry On Fail** (with max tries and wait between), **Continue On Fail** / *Continue (using error output)* which gives the node a second output wired to your error path, and a workflow-level **Error Workflow** setting — a separate workflow that runs automatically whenever this one fails, receiving the error details. Combined with the **Error Trigger** node, you can build one centralized error handler shared by every workflow you own. **Zapier** has **Autoreplay** (automatic retries on certain errors, paid plans), error emails, and the pattern of a dedicated "error catcher" Zap fed by an explicit path. The mental model is the same as `try/catch` in code: wrap the risky operation, decide what to do when it throws, and never let an unhandled failure end the run silently. ##### Retries and exponential backoff For transient failures, retrying is the whole answer — but *how* you retry matters. Naive retries make things worse. If a service is overloaded and 500 clients all retry immediately, you have created a stampede that keeps it down. **Exponential backoff** spaces attempts out geometrically: ```text attempt 1 → fail → wait 1s attempt 2 → fail → wait 2s attempt 3 → fail → wait 4s attempt 4 → fail → wait 8s attempt 5 → fail → give up: log, alert, dead-letter ``` Add **jitter** — a small random offset — so simultaneous clients do not synchronize their retries: ```javascript // n8n Code node: compute a backoff delay with jitter const attempt = $json.attempt ?? 1; const baseMs = 1000; const maxMs = 60000; const backoff = Math.min(baseMs * Math.pow(2, attempt - 1), maxMs); const jitter = Math.random() * backoff * 0.3; // up to 30% randomness const waitMs = Math.round(backoff + jitter); return [{ json: { ...$json, attempt: attempt + 1, wait_ms: waitMs, give_up: attempt >= 5, }, }]; ``` Two rules constrain retries: **Only retry what is retryable.** 429 and 5xx: yes. 4xx (other than 429): no — the request is malformed and will be just as malformed next time. Honour a `Retry-After` header when the server sends one. **Only retry what is safe to repeat.** Which brings us to the most important concept of the day. ##### Idempotency An operation is **idempotent** if performing it twice has the same effect as performing it once. `GET` is naturally idempotent. "Set status to shipped" is idempotent. "Create an order" and "charge ₹4,998" are emphatically not. This matters because retries, webhook redeliveries and manual re-runs all cause the same event to be processed more than once. Without idempotency, your reliability mechanism becomes a duplication machine — exactly what happened to those two double-shipped orders. Three techniques, roughly in order of preference: **1. Idempotency keys.** Many good APIs (Stripe, Razorpay) accept an `Idempotency-Key` header. Send a stable key derived from the event — the order ID, not a random UUID — and the API guarantees that repeated requests with the same key produce one effect and return the original response. ```bash curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/charges \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Idempotency-Key: order-ORD-1042" \ -d '{"amount": 499800, "currency": "inr"}' ``` **2. Check-before-write.** Search the destination for the record first; create only if absent. This is the search-then-update-or-create pattern from CRM day, now serving a reliability purpose. **3. A processed-events store.** Keep a table (Make Data Store, Airtable, Postgres, Redis) of event IDs you have handled. At the top of the workflow, look up the incoming ID and stop if it is present; at the end, record it. This works even against APIs with no idempotency support. ##### Fallbacks and default values Not every failure deserves to stop the run. **Fallbacks** let a workflow degrade gracefully: - Enrichment API down → proceed with the un-enriched record and tag it `enrichment_pending`. - `company` field missing → default to `"Unknown"` rather than failing validation. - Primary notification channel unavailable → fall back to email. - Geocoding failed → store the raw address and flag it for later. The discipline is to distinguish **essential** from **optional** steps at design time. Ask of each step: *if this fails, is the whole run worthless?* If not, give it a fallback and continue. In n8n this is *Continue On Fail* plus a Set node supplying defaults; in Make it is an error handler with a *Resume* directive. ##### Alerting on failures An alert nobody sees is not a safety net. Good alerting has four properties: - **Reaches a human who can act** — a channel people actually read, with an ownership mention for urgent cases. - **Contains enough context to diagnose without opening the platform**: workflow name, execution ID/link, the failing step, the error message, the record identifier, and the timestamp. - **Is deduplicated.** A loop failing 300 times should produce one alert saying "300 failures," not 300 alerts. Track a hash of the error and suppress repeats within a window. - **Distinguishes severity.** Payment sync failed → ping immediately. Optional enrichment failed → daily digest. A useful alert body looks like this: ```json { "severity": "high", "workflow": "shopify-to-warehouse-sync", "execution_id": "e_88213", "failed_step": "HTTP Request: create shipment", "error": "503 Service Unavailable", "record": { "order_id": "ORD-1042", "customer": "ananya@example.com" }, "attempts": 5, "occurred_at": "2026-03-14T09:12:44+05:30", "action": "Order queued in retry sheet; will auto-retry hourly" } ``` That last field — what the system already did about it — is what turns an alert into something a human can triage in ten seconds. ##### The reliable workflow pattern ```mermaid flowchart TD T[Trigger: event arrives] --> D{Already processed?
check event ID store} D -->|yes| X[Stop: duplicate] D -->|no| V{Validate required fields} V -->|invalid| L1[Log to error sheet
+ digest alert] V -->|valid| A[Main action
retry 5x, backoff + jitter] A -->|success| M[Mark event ID processed] A -->|transient, retries exhausted| Q[Queue for later retry
+ high-severity alert] A -->|permanent 4xx| L2[Log with payload
+ high-severity alert] M --> N[Optional enrichment
fallback on failure] N --> Z[Done] ``` Note the shape: deduplicate at the front, validate before acting, retry only the retryable, record success as the last step of the critical path, and treat optional work as optional. ##### Common pitfalls - **Alert step placed after the failing step** — it never runs. Put alerting on the error path, not the happy path. - **Retrying non-idempotent operations** without a key or check — duplicates. - **Infinite retries** — always cap attempts. - **Catching everything and continuing silently** — the worst failure mode, because the automation appears healthy while quietly losing data. - **Marking the event processed before the work succeeds** — a crash in between loses it permanently. - **No dead-letter destination** — failed records must land somewhere reviewable, not vanish. - **Alert storms** with no deduplication, which recreate the muted-channel problem. - **Never testing failure.** Deliberately break your workflow: revoke a token, send a malformed payload, point at a dead URL. Untested error handling is not error handling. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: take an existing workflow and add **three** things — a retry on a flaky step, a fallback for a missing field, and an alert message to yourself if the workflow ultimately fails. Then *prove each one works* by causing the failure deliberately. Temporarily change an API URL to something invalid and watch the retry-then-alert sequence unfold. The mini project is a genuinely production-shaped build: an **API-sync workflow** with a dedicated error-handling route that retries transient failures, logs permanent failures to a sheet, sends an alert, and is **idempotent so re-runs never create duplicates**. Test idempotency explicitly — run the same input three times and confirm exactly one record exists at the end. That test is the deliverable that will impress an interviewer. For the assignment, list **five failure modes and the strategy for each**. A strong answer maps them cleanly: rate limit → retry with backoff; server outage → retry then queue and alert; missing optional field → fallback default; malformed record → skip, log, digest alert; duplicate event → idempotency check. Justify each choice by whether the failure is transient, permanent, or data-related. ##### Key takeaways - Classify failures as transient (retry), permanent (log and alert), or data-related (skip with a fallback) — each needs a different response. - Use platform error handlers as try/catch: Make's directives, n8n's Retry On Fail and Error Workflows, Zapier's Autoreplay plus an error path. - Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, cap the attempts, honour `Retry-After`, and never retry a 4xx that is not a 429. - Idempotency is what makes retries safe: use idempotency keys, check-before-write, or a processed-events store. - Alerts must reach someone who can act, carry diagnostic context, be deduplicated, and be tested by deliberately breaking the workflow.
